extracted.intended_audience: patent and trademark practitioners before the USPTO; attorneys subject to OED discipline; counsel handling trademark prosecution
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and disciplinary criteria governing attorney conduct in trademark prosecution before the USPTO, particularly duties when preparing and submitting verified statements and responses (e.g., Section 2(f) distinctiveness claims) and handling adverse evidence. Includes applicable rules, evidentiary expectations, and potential sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicable professional conduct rules (timing-based applicability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events occurring prior to May 3, 2013 are governed by the USPTO Code of Professional Responsibility (37 C.F.R. § 10.20 et seq.); effective May 3, 2013 the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.101–11.901) apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must determine which regulatory regime applies based on the dates of the conduct at issue; discipline is assessed under the applicable rules for that timeframe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on signing papers filed in violation of § 11.18
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not sign a paper filed in the Office in violation of the provisions of § 11.18 (cited as proscribed by 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(15)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signing a verified statement or filing that does not comply with the verification/signature requirements or that contains false material representations can constitute professional misconduct. The Final Order cites the rule as a basis for discipline in this case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to handle legal matters with preparation adequate in the circumstances (reasonable inquiry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must conduct an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances and have preparation adequate to the matter before handling it or submitting filings (37 C.F.R. § 10.77(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequate preparation includes examining evidence in the practitioner's possession that may be contrary to representations made to the Office. Failing to make a reasonable inquiry or to prepare adequately before submitting sworn statements is misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to examine potentially contrary evidence in possession before making factual assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: If a practitioner has evidence in their possession that may contradict a factual claim (e.g., that a mark is non-generic or has acquired distinctiveness), the practitioner must examine that evidence before submitting or signing sworn statements asserting the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: relying on folder labels or ignoring exhibits without review. Example from the Final Order: Respondent received folders labeled 'generic references' and did not examine the materials, which was deemed unreasonable preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to disclose adverse correspondence/evidence to the client
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must forward to and advise their clients of adverse correspondence and evidence relevant to the matter (e.g., opposing counsel's letters and attached exhibits showing third-party uses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to share such materials with the client (or otherwise advising them of adverse evidence) undermines informed client decisions and can be misconduct; Respondent's failure to forward Corporation's letter/exhibits was cited as misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for Section 2(f) acquired distinctiveness claims/declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: To amend an application under Section 2(f) and claim acquired distinctiveness, the evidence/declaration must support that the mark has 'become distinctive' through substantially exclusive and continuous use and, where required, specifically attest that distinctiveness existed prior to the date of the declaration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Examining Attorney deemed an earlier declaration insufficient because it did not specifically attest that the mark had acquired distinctiveness prior to the date of the declaration. Practitioners must ensure the declaration meets the Office's evidentiary and attestation requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on procuring registration by fraud / material misrepresentation with intent to deceive
rubrics_metrics.description: A trademark registration procured by a false and material misrepresentation made with intent to deceive the USPTO may be cancelled and gives rise to potential discipline; the factfinder may require proof by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: jury found by clear and convincing evidence that the registration was obtained by fraud based on a false claim of acquired distinctiveness. Practitioners must avoid knowingly or recklessly making material misrepresentations to the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of criminal and civil penalties for false statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Sworn statements filed with the USPTO often include language warning that willful false statements are punishable under 18 U.S.C. § 1001 and may jeopardize validity of documents/applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners signing or submitting such statements must ensure their truthfulness; ignorance of contrary evidence is not a defense where a reasonable inquiry would have revealed problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and future considerations for disciplinary records
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions for misconduct may include reprimand (private or public), publication of a redacted Final Order, and notice in the Official Gazette. The Office may consider disciplinary records in future complaints or proceedings, including as aggravating evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should understand that even a private reprimand can be published in redacted form, and that the record may be used by the Office if similar misconduct is later alleged or in determining severity of future sanctions.
